title: Baron FitzGibbon

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2106x3400px open-access image (region x=0.6026, y=0.7353, w=0.2996, h=0.1397)

description: A fearless politician who engineered the act of uniting Ireland with England, FitzGibbon was the newly appointed Lord Chancellor of Ireland (whose duties included that of chief judge) when Stuart painted his portrait. The crownlike upper portion of FitzGibbon's mace, or ceremonial staff, is seen on the table at the right. Propped against the table is a satin and velvet purse embroidered with the royal coat of arms.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: This portrait was painted on a large piece of textured linen, likely a tablecloth.

title: After the Bath

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 3400x2297px open-access image (region x=0.2459, y=0.4506, w=0.4209, h=0.4693)

description: Mary Cassatt began using pastel in the 1870s and continued to experiment with the medium throughout her career. This drawing depicts a mother and child, one of the artist's preferred subjects. Cassatt typically used the technique seen here, in which she finished her sitters' faces with a high degree of detail but rendered the rest of the composition in a much looser and sketchier style.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: Mary Cassatt once commented that pastel was "the most satisfactory medium for [portraying] children," since they could not sit still for long and the medium allowed for rapid sketching.

title: Courtesan Dreaming of her Childhood
medium: Woodblock print; ink and color on paper
description: This print depicts a courtesan dreaming about the time she was taken from her family to become a courtesan. The man leading the girl by the hand is probably escorting her to the Yoshiwara, the entertainment district in Edo. This format is called a pillar print, or hashira-e (literally, "pillar picture").
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: Pillar prints, or hashira-e (柱絵), are long and narrow Japanese woodblock prints originally intended to decorate wooden pillars.

title: Portrait of Dora Wheeler

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 3400x3254px open-access image (region x=0.6626, y=0.1156, w=0.2, h=0.1567)

description: Dora Wheeler became Chase's first student when he returned from overseas study in Munich and set up a teaching studio in New York. At the time, few American artists accepted women as private pupils. After her course of study, Wheeler joined her mother in launching a successful decorating firm, one of the first businesses in the country to be operated entirely by women.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: Chase and Wheeler worked together to raise money for constructing the Statue of Liberty's pedestal.

title: Elizabeth Beltzhoover Mason

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2805x3400px open-access image (region x=0.293, y=0.6479, w=0.3005, h=0.1853)

description: The sitter’s high-waisted dress, pearl necklace, and elegant hairstyle of cascading ringlets reflect the height of fashion around 1800. Her gaze is assured: her chin is tilted upward but her eyes peer down with confidence. Mason’s husband was a prosperous lawyer, an influential figure in President Thomas Jefferson’s administration, and a plantation owner in Maryland.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: Stuart also painted a portrait of George Washington, now immortalized on the dollar bill.

title: Peasant Returning from the Manure Heap
artistBio: Son of a wealthy farmer, Jean-François Millet studied with a portrait painter from Cherbourg, Bon du Mouchel (1807-1846), himself a student of David. Mouchel required his young apprentice to copy paintings in the museum in Cherbourg, where Millet had been sent to enter the studio of Lucien-Théophile Langlois (1803-1845), a former student of Gros.

artistBioSource.name: Cleveland Museum of Art — artist biography

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2777x3400px open-access image (region x=0.2578, y=0.3709, w=0.301, h=0.1853)

description: Millet moved from Paris to the nearby village of Barbizon in 1849 in search of rustic subject matter. The group of painters working in the countryside surrounding the Forest of Fontainebleau frequently painted out-of-doors in order to create fresh and accurate views of nature. While most of the Barbizon artists focused primarily on landscape, Millet also represented peasants.

title: The Garden

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2602x3400px open-access image (region x=0.3405, y=0.3791, w=0.2998, h=0.1729)

description: Part of an expatriate community in Venice, James McNeill Whistler focused on the city’s architectural details in the prints, drawings, and paintings that he made during a year spent living there. This etching presents a private garden from the perspective of one of the city’s distinctive canals. Seen through an open doorway, the view, offers a voyeuristic glimpse of its inhabitants’ lives.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: This print is among the only ones in James McNeill Whistler's Second Venice Set without a clearly identifiable setting.

title: The Last Supper

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2336x3400px open-access image (region x=0.3878, y=0.6291, w=0.1999, h=0.1041)

description: In this compact scene, Lucas van Leyden offered a condensed view of the Last Supper, focusing on Christ and Saint John—the Beloved Apostle—on the far side of the table and Judas—the apostle who would betray Christ—on the near side. Wine flows freely, mixing hints of its symbolic significance with a certain hunger for drink as shown by the disciple who receives a replenishment in the foreground.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: This image is smaller than most smart phones, inviting the viewer to lean in and look closely.

title: Black-Figure Neck-Amphora of Panathenaic Shape (Storage Vessel)

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2644x3400px open-access image (region x=0.177, y=0.1668, w=0.3003, h=0.175)

description: The narrow neck and base of amphorae of this shape probably derive from vessels used to transport oil and wine long distances. Here, the painted decoration accentuates the shape, with simple rays at the base, tongues on the shoulder, and a double lotus-and-palmette chain on the neck. Added red rings separate these patterns, with black gloss covering most of the exterior; only the upper surface of the mouth is reserved.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: The shape of this amphora mimics those of larger, figured prize vases.

title: Early Morning After a Storm at Sea

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 3400x2050px open-access image (region x=0.1291, y=0.3839, w=0.4209, h=0.5259)

description: The powerful Atlantic surf pounding against the desolate coast of Prouts Neck, Maine, provided primary subject matter for the dramatic paintings that Homer created during his final decades. This example, which the artist proclaimed as "the best picture of the sea that I have painted," was initially conceived as a watercolor.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: Winslow Homer's studio in Prouts Neck, Maine, is a National Historic Landmark.

title: Bacchanal with Silenus

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 3400x2267px open-access image (region x=0.2126, y=0.4063, w=0.2, h=0.225)

description: This print was probably conceived by Andrea Mantegna as the right side of Bacchanal with a Wine Vat, which shows Bacchus crowned. Here, the central figure is also crowned, but unlike the wine god, he appears saturated with drink. The scene may come from the Roman poet Virgil (70–19 BCE).
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: Like most artists in Renaissance Italy, Mantegna was often inspired by ancient Greek and Roman art. In this print, the revelers are positioned in the foreground of a shallow picture plane, reminding savvy viewers of a Roman frieze.

title: Rue Transnonain, April 15, 1834
artistBio: Honoré Daumier was eight years old when his father, a glazier and frame maker who had decided to pursue his poetic talents in Paris, sent for the wife and three sons he lad left behind in Marseilles. In Paris Daumier studied drawing with Alexandre Lenoir (1761-1839) and at the Académie Suisse.

artistBioSource.name: Cleveland Museum of Art — artist biography

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 3400x2396px open-access image (region x=0.5459, y=0.1273, w=0.2, h=0.2129)

description: Although it supported the French middle class, the government of Louis-Philippe (1773–1850) oppressed workers. The rebellion of the silk weavers of Lyon, who toiled 18 hours a day for a pittance, touched off a sympathetic revolt in Paris. During the uprising, sniper fire directed toward government troops emanated from a house on the Rue Transnonain.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: Although government censors approved publication of this print, they seized it upon its exhibition in a Parisian print shop.

title: Table Fountain

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 3033x3400px open-access image (region x=0.2756, y=0.4582, w=0.299, h=0.2)

description: Conceptually and stylistically, this object is beyond all else a piece of Gothic architecture in miniature with vaults, pinnacles, columns, and traceried arches. Though the artist who created it is unknown, he was unquestionably inspired by the great Gothic buildings of his time. The table fountain is a three-tiered assembly combining cast elements with bent sheets of gilt-silver.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: This fountain with its minute architectural details and finely made enamel plaques displayed the wealth and refinement of the owner as it entertained his guests. Imagine hearing the ringing of the tiny bells when this fountain was in use.

title: Eight Views of Kanazawa at Night

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 3400x1681px open-access image (region x=0.1626, y=0.2487, w=0.4209, h=0.6413)

description: Late in his career, Hiroshige explored the poetic theme of setsugekka, “snow, moon, and flowers,” in a set of three triptychs. This panoramic scene shows the autumn moon over Kanazawa, near Tokyo. Hiroshige’s contemporaries would have recognized the coastline dotted with villages, fishing boats, and the distinctive double-arched bridge at the bottom right.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: The red cartouche on the right gives the title of the print, while the artist’s signature and red seal are on the far left.

title: The Presentation in the Temple
artistBio: French Rococo artist who epitomizes the frivolous and elegant court life of France in the mid-18th century. During his early career he was closely associated with Watteau, many of whose paintings he engraved.

artistBioSource.name: Cleveland Museum of Art — artist biography

medium: pen and brown ink, brush and brown wash, and black chalk, heightened with white paint; framing lines in pen and brown ink

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 1307x2048px open-access image (region x=0.6174, y=0.6519, w=0.3007, h=0.1436)

description: Late in his career, François Boucher adopted a drawing style characterized by strong pen lines and loosely brushed washes. This sheet, which dates from that period, depicts the blind priest Simeon, at left, who was promised that he would see the Messiah before his death. When the Christ child was brought into the temple near him, Simeon regained his sight.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: This drawing was probably a sketch for an oil painting that Boucher was unable to complete before his death.

title: Adam and Eve in Paradise

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2376x3400px open-access image (region x=0.367, y=0.1791, w=0.3013, h=0.1582)

description: Lucas Cranach’s Eden shows the first couple just prior to tasting the forbidden fruit. Adam holds one fruit, and Eve plucks a second from the tree of knowledge. The composition is packed with stags, horses, sheep, and a lion, ram, and boar.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: The coats of arms hanging from the tree in this image are those of the artist's patron, Frederick, Elector of Saxony (1463–1525).

title: Miss Loïe Fuller

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2316x3400px open-access image (region x=0.1252, y=0.5897, w=0.4188, h=0.2147)

description: Parisian audiences were captivated by Loïe Fuller (1862–1928), the American dancer seen in this print, whose unique performances involved manipulating voluminous translucent gowns with the aid of large poles in each hand. Fuller danced in a specially designed space featuring a glass floor illuminated from below and surrounded by mirrors.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: Loïe Fuller, depicted here, donated a group of sculptures to the Cleveland Museum of Art following its opening to the public in 1916.

title: Views: The Canal Lock at Dolo

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 3400x2375px open-access image (region x=0.4291, y=0.4387, w=0.3, h=0.3225)

description: Antonio Canaletto took up etching as an extension of his painting practice, which consisted of representing topographical views of Venice for wealthy patrons. This print belongs to a series he made of rural scenery outside the city—here, the village of Dolo and its canal.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: Dolo, the town depicted here, was a popular site of country homes for wealthy inhabitants of Venice nearby.

title: St. Jerome Seated near a Pollard Willow

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2961x3400px open-access image (region x=0.1125, y=0.4, w=0.4211, h=0.275)

description: Of the hundreds of prints Albrecht Dürer made, only three were drypoints, in which a needle scratched directly into a copperplate creates velvety, fuzzy lines. In this image of Saint Jerome, Dürer exploited these qualities of drypoint to manifest the natural, spiritual realm of the saint’s hermitage in the wilderness. Jerome pauses from his studies to pray in a setting that buzzes with life.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: This is one of only three prints Albrecht Dürer made using drypoint, in which a needle is scratched directly into the copperplate.

title: Maruru (Offerings of Gratitude)
artistBio: Gauguin spent the first seven years of his life with his mother and great uncle in Peru. In 1855 his mother took him back to France where he attended boarding school.

artistBioSource.name: Cleveland Museum of Art — artist biography

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 3400x1965px open-access image (region x=0.4459, y=0.2239, w=0.4209, h=0.5486)

description: In 1891 Paul Gauguin traveled to Tahiti, seeking a more authentic style of art making than the conservatism he rejected in Western culture. After returning to Paris in 1893, he began working on Noa Noa, an illustrated book that explained and illustrated his experiences abroad. Although the project was never completed, this print is one of its illustrations.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: The majority of prints from Noa Noa were printed by the master printer Louis Roy or, later, by Paul Gauguin's son Pola, making this impression particularly rare.

title: The Last Supper

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2521x3400px open-access image (region x=0.4831, y=0.4418, w=0.4213, h=0.2353)

description: The Christian sacrament of the Eucharist is traced to the Last Supper, when Christ said of the wine, “This is my blood.” For artists, the scene was full of both symbolic and narrative potential. Albrecht Dürer created a compact, vertical composition that focuses on the closeness of the disciples and the moment, wine flowing, when Christ reveals his fate.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: This print depicts the apostles dining on a humble but sturdy refectory table. Dürer included the date of the print on the middle trestle, a location often reserved for heraldry on more lavish tables.

title: A Woman Clothed with the Sun
alternativeTitles: The Apocalypse of Saint John: A Woman Clothed with the Sun
artistBio: A leader of the symbolist movement in France, Odilon Redon was born in Bordeaux in 1840 and grew up in the surrounding region. During his early years he studied drawing, architecture, and the violin.

artistBioSource.name: Cleveland Museum of Art — artist biography

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2669x3400px open-access image (region x=0.2548, y=0.6918, w=0.199, h=0.1168)

description: The last of Odilon Redon’s 11 lithographic portfolios, this series relates to the Book of Revelation from the Christian Bible. The subject had been explored throughout art history, allowing the artist to align himself with past masters, such as Albrecht Dürer.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: This is one of the last works where Redon experimented with lithograph and all-black medium. In contrast, bright, dazzling colors characterize his late works.

title: The Holy Family with Mary Magdalen

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2586x3400px open-access image (region x=0.244, y=0.2541, w=0.4192, h=0.2397)

description: The seemingly weightless figures, the startling color combinations, and the moody, imprecise setting all show El Greco’s interest in conveying the intense spirituality of these figures rather than their concrete reality. Above all, the painting addresses Mary’s role as mediator between Christ and the viewer. She supports her son, but her faraway look indicates awareness of his fate.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: The nearly levitating body of the Christ child further emphasizes the ethereal setting of the Holy Family.

title: Orpheus
artistBio: A leader of the symbolist movement in France, Odilon Redon was born in Bordeaux in 1840 and grew up in the surrounding region. During his early years he studied drawing, architecture, and the violin.

artistBioSource.name: Cleveland Museum of Art — artist biography

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2802x3400px open-access image (region x=0.3291, y=0.3271, w=0.1999, h=0.1229)

description: Drawn in vivid layers of pastel crayon, this work depicts the head of the poet and musician Orpheus. The story of the god of music, whose music carried on after his death through his lyre and head, fascinated Redon, who related to Orpheus's dedication to his art.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: Another version of this pastel (now in the collection of the Musée Fabre de Montpellier) was part of a group of later works by Redon shown at the 1913 International Exhibition of Modern Art—better known as the Armory Show—which introduced the artist to American audiences.

title: Nymphs and a Satyr (Amor Vincit Omnia)

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 3400x2580px open-access image (region x=0.1291, y=0.1236, w=0.3, h=0.2965)

description: Like his colleague Claude Lorrain, Poussin depicted historical and mythological subjects in landscapes inspired by the countryside around Rome. His themes were often complex, and frequently incorporated witty allusions to classical texts. Here, a playful cupid tugs Pan, the goatlegged Greek god of the woods, toward Venus, the goddess of love.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: After arriving in Rome and experiencing financial instability, Nicolas Poussin turned to painting more popular, lucrative mythological scenes, such as those depicting nymphs and satyrs.

title: Bacchanal with a Wine Vat

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 3400x2342px open-access image (region x=0.0959, y=0.1998, w=0.2, h=0.2182)

description: Andrea Mantegna was among the first artists in Italy to produce engravings. His scene of a bacchanalia, a wine-fueled festival of ancient Rome, is composed as if on a shallow stage, attesting to Mantegna’s interest in relief-carved Roman sarcophagi (stone coffins). Standing with his horn of plenty, Bacchus is in control of his senses.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: Philosophers and moralists cautioned against drinking straight from the vat, because, as Bacchus's exalted pose suggests, only a god could handle such an intoxicating drink. Mere mortals usually mixed their wine with water until the 1800s.

title: A Winter Sky

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 3400x2476px open-access image (region x=0.2126, y=0.3772, w=0.2, h=0.2056)

description: In A Winter Sky, George Inness concentrated on depicting the effects of light and atmosphere. In this composition, the artist combined a vibrant, glowing sunset with a harsh, bleak landscape. Inness's color choice reinforces this contrast, as the warm pinks and yellows in the sky play off the cool blues of the frozen ground.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: George Inness originally included a figure standing at the left edge of the pond, which he later painted over so that it is no longer visible.

title: Madame Désiré Raoul-Rochette
artistBio: A leading exponent of French neoclassicism and the academic tradition, Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres was born in Montauban in 1780. At the age of ten he began studying art and music in Toulouse.

artistBioSource.name: Cleveland Museum of Art — artist biography

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2692x3400px open-access image (region x=0.3158, y=0.0918, w=0.4209, h=0.25)

description: While living in Rome, Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres began making commissioned graphite portraits as a way of providing additional income. He aspired to a career as a history painter, however, and made such works only as gifts for friends after achieving professional success. This sheet was a gift for its sitter's husband, a famous archaeologist to whom Ingres dedicated it at lower right.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: Ingres paid close attention to his sitter's costume: a fashionable open coat and dress with leg-of-mutton sleeves.

title: Portrait of Agostino Barbarigo

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 3400x3331px open-access image (region x=0.2126, y=0.2852, w=0.3, h=0.2297)

description: Barbarigo served as second in command of the Venetian naval forces during the Battle of Lepanto, fighting against the Ottoman Empire on October 7, 1571. During the skirmish, Barbarigo was slain by a Turkish arrow, which he holds in the portrait.Barbarigo’s identity is defined by his military prowess.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: The arrow symbolically indicates that this portrait was painted after the sitter died in battle.

title: Study for "The Romancer" (Le Conteur)
medium: red chalk; red and black chalk (upper left figure)

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2664x3400px open-access image (region x=0.5105, y=0.3918, w=0.3007, h=0.1771)

description: This sheet was a preparatory study for the painting The Romancer. An actor in the costume of Mezzetin, a stock character of the commedia dell’arte (a type of satirical theatrical entertainment of Italian origin popular in aristocratic circles in 18th-century France), interrupts a guitarist with a bold sexual advance.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: Jean Antoine Watteau likely drew this sheet from a combination of life study and imagination, working from a model and adding other elements of his own creation.

title: Sarcophagus

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 3400x1569px open-access image (region x=0.6126, y=0.1536, w=0.3, h=0.4888)

description: The tragic figure Orestes appears three times on the front of this sarcophagus, always wielding a short sword. In the center he stands over the body of his mother Clytemnestra, and at center left over the body of her lover Aegisthus. Orestes has killed them both to avenge their murder of his father Agamemnon, upon his return from years of fighting at Troy.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: From the Greek word for “flesh-eating,” sarcophagus is now used generically for “coffin.”

title: Dance of Death: The Miser

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2402x3400px open-access image (region x=0.1682, y=0.5541, w=0.301, h=0.1603)

description: Dance of Death is the most celebrated series of woodcuts designed by Holbein. The forty-one blocks were cut by Hans Lützelburger in the years immediately before his death in 1526, though the set was not published until 1538. Dance of Death originated as a drama in the middle of the 14th century.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)

title: Outskirts of Paris
artistBio: Self-taught artist Henri Rousseau was born in Laval in 1844. He entered the military at the age of eighteen and served as a saxophone player in an infantry band.

artistBioSource.name: Cleveland Museum of Art — artist biography

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 3400x2799px open-access image (region x=0.2791, y=0.6277, w=0.3, h=0.2733)

description: In addition to his large jungle scenes, Rousseau also painted small landscapes, including this view of a river or canal on the outskirts of Paris. license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: Rousseau once said to Picasso: "We are the two greatest artists of this era, you in the Egyptian style, I in the modern style."

title: Capriccio: A Palace with a Courtyard by the Lagoon

culture: Northwestern India, Rajasthan, Rajput Kingdom of Mewar

title: Portrait of Isabella Brant

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2877x3400px open-access image (region x=0.3545, y=0.2832, w=0.4213, h=0.2668)

title: Salome with the Head of St. John the Baptist
medium: pen and brown ink and brush and brown wash and white gouache; framing lines in pen and black ink

description: Salome's story is described in the biblical Gospels of Mark and Matthew. After dancing for King Herod of Galilee, her new stepfather, she was granted any wish she desired. license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: The artist colored the paper on this drawing a dark brown in order to emphasize the highlights and shadows created with inks.

title: Fight Between a Tiger and a Buffalo
artistBio: Self-taught artist Henri Rousseau was born in Laval in 1844. He entered the military at the age of eighteen and served as a saxophone player in an infantry band.

artistBioSource.name: Cleveland Museum of Art — artist biography

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 3400x3046px open-access image (region x=0.4959, y=0.3769, w=0.3, h=0.2511)

description: Having never ventured outside France, Henri Rousseau derived his jungle scenes from reading travel books and visiting the Paris botanical garden. He placed this imaginary scene of a tiger attacking a buffalo within a fantastic jungle environment in which botanical accuracy was of little importance (note the bananas growing upside down). Here, sharply outlined hothouse plants are enlarged to fearsome proportions.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: Many of Henri Rousseau's paintings depict wild animals and tropical jungles that might lead one to believe he traveled widely. However, Rousseau never left France, but drew inspiration from visiting botanical gardens and reading travel books.

title: Pontifical Ceremony in Saints Giovanni e Paolo, Venice, 1782

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 3400x2523px open-access image (region x=0.0791, y=0.5057, w=0.3, h=0.3032)

title: Head of a Tahitian Woman
artistBio: Gauguin spent the first seven years of his life with his mother and great uncle in Peru. In 1855 his mother took him back to France where he attended boarding school.

artistBioSource.name: Cleveland Museum of Art — artist biography

medium: graphite with stumping and graphite wash on parchment

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2715x3400px open-access image (region x=0.3002, y=0.2668, w=0.4203, h=0.2521)

description: This drawing belongs to a group of highly finished portrait drawings of Tahitians made by Paul Gauguin shortly after his arrival in the South Seas. While getting used to this new place, Gauguin initially avoided painting, preferring first to familiarize himself with the landscape and people through observation and drawing. The meticulous quality of this graphite study suggests that it was made from life.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: In his writings, Gauguin often referred to his drawings as "documents"—records of motifs and ideas he could use later.

title: Mount Vesuvius at Midnight

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 3400x2394px open-access image (region x=0.3959, y=0.5058, w=0.3, h=0.3195)

description: For centuries, artists and tourists have been attracted to Mount Vesuvius, a volcano near Naples. While living in London in 1868, Albert Bierstadt heard that the volcano was active once again, and rushed immediately to Italy. It is not certain that he actually saw an eruption, although the resultant painting presents a convincing image of spewing lava and ash.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: This painting is a smaller version of a much larger canvas that is now lost.

title: Peasant Girl with Dog
artistBio: Renoir's parents, a tailor and a dressmaker, moved their family to Paris in 1844. At age thirteen Renoir apprenticed with the porcelain decorators Levy Frères & Cie.

artistBioSource.name: Cleveland Museum of Art — artist biography

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 1536x1976px open-access image (region x=0.1445, y=0.2794, w=0.4212, h=0.246)

description: During the last decades of his career, Renoir worked prolifically in red chalk, which was used to develop a loose and sketchy style. In this drawing, the artist attempted to recapture the spontaneity that characterized Impressionist art a few decades earlier. By showing a young girl seated resting peacefully alongside a bale of hay, he idealized rural French life.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: The art historian John Rewald supposedly called this work "one of the two or three most beautiful Renoir drawings in America."

title: A Hussar Officer on Horseback

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2704x3400px open-access image (region x=0.081, y=0.3291, w=0.301, h=0.1791)

description: John Singleton Copley left Boston at the start of the American Revolution in 1775 to pursue his career in England, where he achieved distinction both as a portraitist and a history painter. license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: The soldier wears a heavy military headdress called a “busby,” originally worn by Hungarian hussars and adopted by American hussar (light cavalry) regiments during the 1800s.

title: The Holy Family (Christ in the Lap of Truth)
alternativeTitles: Christ in the Lap of Truth
medium: black, gray, and brown ink applied with pen and point of brush; gray, pink, yellow, and green wash

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2942x3400px open-access image (region x=0.2315, y=0.2541, w=0.1999, h=0.1291)

description: Although he rejected institutionalized religion, Blake was intensely spiritual, and much of his art was inspired by a highly personal reading of the Bible or by literature based upon it, such as John Milton’s Paradise Lost (1667). license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: This drawing was first owned by Thomas Butts, an English civil servant who became William Blake's most important patron and supporter for about two decades.

title: Portrait of a Man, Possibly Girolamo Rosati

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 3139x3400px open-access image (region x=0.3476, y=0.1668, w=0.201, h=0.1397)

description: The gesture of the elegantly dressed man is a mystery. Is he rising from his chair to address someone or is he pointing to something outside the frame? His right hand rests on a piece of paper (a letter?), while on the table are clover—a symbol of abundance, good fortune, and happy marriage—and jasmine, associated with purity and love, further emphasized by the roses on the trellis.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: This fashionable man broadcasts his wealth by wearing a fur-lined velvet and satin outfit with expensive gold jewelry.

title: Buddha of the Future (Miroku Bosatsu)
medium: cast bronze, incised, with traces of gilding

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2608x3400px open-access image (region x=0.3723, y=0.7418, w=0.2991, h=0.1729)

description: Buddhism was introduced to Japan in the sixth century. For early Japanese devotees, Buddhism offered the promise of salvation through faith in the Buddha of the Future, who would appear at the end of the world. The concept of eternal salvation held particular resonance with the Japanese aristocracy, who became the staunchest supporters of this new faith.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: The Sanskrit name of this being, Maitreya, derives from the Sanskrit word for friend, mita.

title: Reading
alternativeTitles: The Artist's Sister, Mme. Pontillon, Seated on the Grass
artistBio: Born into a prosperous family, Berthe Morisot was encouraged at an early age to become an amateur artist. Along with her sister Edma, she began her studies with Geoffroy-Alphonse Chocarne (act. 1838-1857), a painter trained in the neoclassical tradition.

artistBioSource.name: Cleveland Museum of Art — artist biography

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 3400x2174px open-access image (region x=0.1959, y=0.1076, w=0.4209, h=0.4949)

description: Morisot’s sister, Edma, posed for this painting of a woman seated on her shawl in a field, her eyes on the pages of a book, with a parasol and fan discarded on the grass.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: The Impressionists were mostly men with a few notable exceptions, including Berthe Morisot. While Morisot's work includes many of the hallmarks of Impressionism, such as her loose brushwork, the subject matter of her paintings often reflects the social constraints of her gender.

title: Young Woman Arranging Her Earring
artistBio: Renoir's parents, a tailor and a dressmaker, moved their family to Paris in 1844. At age thirteen Renoir apprenticed with the porcelain decorators Levy Frères & Cie.

description: During his later years, Pierre-Auguste Renoir moved away from pure Impressionism toward a classicizing style featuring strong, monumental figures of substantial weight and volume. interestingFacts: The model for this painting is Gabrielle Renard—a housekeeper, nursemaid, studio assistant, and frequent model to Renoir.

title: Portrait of a Family Playing Music

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 3400x2867px open-access image (region x=0.5459, y=0.6338, w=0.2, h=0.1782)

description: The identity of the sitters remains unknown, although the marble floor and mantelpiece, the Transylvanian prayer rug on the table, and the silk clothes all point to the family’s considerable wealth. interestingFacts: During this period, the Dutch Republic was the richest, most urbanized nation.

title: Portrait of a Woman

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2523x3400px open-access image (region x=0.0785, y=0.0918, w=0.3004, h=0.1668)

description: Born to a Sephardic Jewish family in Livorno, Italy, Amedeo Modigliani studied briefly in Florence and Venice before moving to Paris in 1906 where he became a key member of the avant-garde art world. license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: Modigliani drew and painted from an early age; when he was 11 years old, his mother predicted that he would become an artist.

title: Sheet of Studies and Sketches
artistBio: Son of a Parisian banker, Edgar Degas enrolled in law school in 1853 following his father's wishes. But he had already shown an interest in art and had also registered to copy at the Louvre.

artistBioSource.name: Cleveland Museum of Art — artist biography

medium: graphite, pen and dark brown ink, and watercolor on thick ivory wove paper

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2645x3400px open-access image (region x=0.1769, y=0.6541, w=0.4208, h=0.2459)

description: Degas traveled to Florence, Italy, in July 1858, where he made this sheet of studies. interestingFacts: The date Degas wrote on this drawing is incorrect; he didn't visit Florence until 1858, and must have inscribed the sheet years later.

title: Saint Peter Repentant

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2769x3400px open-access image (region x=0.2763, y=0.3126, w=0.2994, h=0.1832)

description: During Jesus’s arrest on the night of the Last Supper, the apostle Peter denied knowing him. Although Christ forgave his betrayal, Peter was consumed by guilt. Georges de La Tour represents Peter as an old man, reflecting on his past actions in a state of perpetual repentance.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: The rooster next to Peter is a reference to Jesus's prediction that Peter will betray him, stating: "Before the rooster crows, you will disown me three times."

title: Roman Ruins, Villa Pamfili
medium: Pen and black ink and watercolor with black chalk underdrawing and heightened with white gouache on cream laid paper

description: While living in Italy, Robert developed a fondness for classical architecture, making countless drawings that served as the basis for paintings and prints for decades after he returned to Paris. title: Saint Nicholas of Bari

title: Christ on the Cross

title: Swift Bull from the Ten Swift Bulls
medium: section of a handscroll mounted as a hanging scroll; ink and slight color on paper

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 1788x3400px open-access image (region x=0.127, y=0.6959, w=0.3015, h=0.1188)

description: Across the world, animals once played a much larger role in the transportation of the elite. license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)

title: Head of Amenhotep III Wearing the Blue Crown

title: Candelabrum Stand of a Dancing Maenad

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2684x3400px open-access image (region x=0.3957, y=0.4418, w=0.3007, h=0.1791)

title: Torso of a Kouros

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2846x3400px open-access image (region x=0.3408, y=0.1812, w=0.3011, h=0.1897)

description: Known as a kouros, the ancient Greek word for a youth, this fragmentary statue belongs to a relatively rare type of large-scale stone sculpture made for little more than a century—shortly before 600 BCE to soon after 500 BCE. license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: In antiquity, brightly colored paint would probably have rendered this kouros more lifelike.

title: Saint-Tropez: The Port

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2534x3400px open-access image (region x=0.4175, y=0.1791, w=0.1989, h=0.1103)

description: Signac adapted for the lithographic process the style he and George Seurat (1859-1891) developed in the 1880s for painting: pointillism. Brilliantly colored dots were juxtaposed to produce a full optical tonal range more luminous than can be obtained from pigments mixed on the palette.

title: The Story of Fukutomi
medium: Handscroll; ink and color on paper
description: This handscroll shows the second half of an odd tale in which a ne’er-do-well seeks the path to quick fortune and learns the art of musical flatulence. license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: This scroll is treasured as the second oldest surviving version of this story.

title: Landscape with Two Pines

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 3400x2487px open-access image (region x=0.6791, y=0.1025, w=0.2, h=0.2051)

description: Primarily a painter and draftsman, Albrecht Altdorfer made only nine etchings, which were intended to imitate his drawings. Those he made between 1522 and 1525—printed in very small numbers for a growing market of print collector—are considered the first prints in European art to depict pure landscape without narrative or devotional content. Here, he displayed remarkable freedom of draftsmanship and apparent spontaneity.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: To make this early etching, the artist used an iron plate rather than the more supple copper, which would shortly come to dominate etching technique.

title: Boy with Anchor

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 3400x1931px open-access image (region x=0.2126, y=0.3454, w=0.4209, h=0.5588)

description: In this work from a series of watercolors produced in Gloucester, MA, in the summer of 1873 Winslow Homer evokes the fraught nature of the local fishing industry by focusing not on the perilous work of adults, but rather the children they leave behind. license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: The mottled texture of the sky is an example of Homer’s blotting technique—a subtractive process in which he applied a wash of water, sprinkled some breadcrumbs, and then gently rubbed the paper with his fingers in order to absorb the extra color, leaving behind a granulated texture.

title: The Feast of Herod (recto); Tomyris with the Head of Cyrus (verso)
medium: pen and brown ink, with black and red chalk, touched with white gouache

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 3400x981px open-access image (region x=0.1126, y=0.0795, w=0.3062, h=0.7971)

description: Peter Paul Rubens had a large studio in Antwerp and used drawing to prepare for large paintings as well as to direct the many pupils who assisted him. interestingFacts: The two stories that Rubens depicted on the front and back of this sheet of paper each feature a gruesome death, the result of revenge at the hands of a powerful woman.

title: A Genoese Lady with Her Child

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2265x3400px open-access image (region x=0.1907, y=0.6103, w=0.3002, h=0.15)

description: Prior to the 1600s, large, full-length portraits of wealthy clients usually emphasized the trappings of status above any other qualities. license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: This portrait was a departure from the painting style popular at this time, focusing less on a demonstrative display of wealth and status and more on capturing the essence of the sitter.

title: They Have Flown, Plate 61

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2424x3400px open-access image (region x=0.3069, y=0.4918, w=0.4212, h=0.225)

description: In the print series Los Caprichos, which translates as “caprices” or “artistic fantasies,” Francisco de Goya drew on his expansive imagination to comment on Spanish society. The artist’s critiques are not always clear, and many of the prints are intentionally ambiguous. Here, three witches support a young woman taking flight.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: When Los Caprichos was first published in 1799, the series was sold in a perfumery and liquor shop in Madrid.

title: Claire Campbell
artistBio: Born into a wealthy family, Édouard Manet was encouraged in his artistic curiosity by his uncle and often visited the Louvre with his college friend Antonin Proust. Initially, however, Manet wanted to pursue a naval career.

artistBioSource.name: Cleveland Museum of Art — artist biography

medium: Pastel with oil on fine-weave canvas

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2799x3400px open-access image (region x=0.3115, y=0.1668, w=0.4202, h=0.2603)

description: During the late 1870s, Edouard Manet began to experience health problems that made it difficult for him to work in oil painting. Instead, he began to draw using pastel, a powdery medium that allowed him to render line and color with each stroke. This work is one of numerous portraits that Manet created around this time with the medium.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: Edouard Manet almost always depicted the subjects of his pastel portraits against plain colored backgrounds, as seen in this work.

title: The Illustrated Miraculous Origins of the Yūzū Nenbutsu School

title: Mount Sainte-Victoire
artistBio: The son of a wealthy banker, Cézanne began his studies in Aix-en-Provence at the École Saint-Joseph in 1849, then attended the Collège Bourbon from 1852 until 1858. artistBioSource.name: Cleveland Museum of Art — artist biography

description: During the last 20 years of his life, Cezanne repeatedly painted Mount Sainte-Victoire near his home in Aix-en-Provence in southern France. license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: Cezanne created 36 paintings and 45 watercolors of Mount Sainte-Victoire. He was preoccupied with this subject and painted this mountain repeatedly until his death.

title: The Troubadour

description: The troubadour, a medieval traveling poet and entertainer, was a popular subject in 19th-century French art. Associated with chivalry and courtly love, the theme reflects a broader, romantic fascination with France's medieval past.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: Daumier was called the “Michelangelo of caricature” and especially renowned for his cartoons and drawings satirizing 19th-century French politics and society.

description: In May 1890, Vincent van Gogh arrived in Auvers, a small town north of Paris, where he rented a room at the inn of Arthur Ravoux. title: The Nativity
artistBio: Born in Oudewater (near Gouda), David probably trained in Haarlem. Admitted (as a foreigner) to the painters' guild in 1484, he was active there until his death in 1523.

artistBioSource.name: Cleveland Museum of Art — artist biography

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2360x3400px open-access image (region x=0.153, y=0.7041, w=0.2013, h=0.1041)

description: The nativity was one of the most frequently depicted subjects in western art. The event marks the entrance of Christ into the world and the fulfillment of Old Testament prophecy. In the distance an angel announces the birth of Christ to the shepherds tending their flocks.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)

title: Berthe Morisot with a Muff
artistBio: Born into a wealthy family, Édouard Manet was encouraged in his artistic curiosity by his uncle and often visited the Louvre with his college friend Antonin Proust. Initially, however, Manet wanted to pursue a naval career.

artistBioSource.name: Cleveland Museum of Art — artist biography

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2744x3400px open-access image (region x=0.1112, y=0.6668, w=0.4213, h=0.2541)

description: This is one of two portraits Manet painted of Morisot dressed for winter in a heavy coat and feathered hat. (See Berthe Morisot with a Half Veil, also in this gallery.) Manet’s wide brushstrokes and crosshatchings, which describe areas of shadow, evoke the sketchy quality of Morisot’s own paintings, likely Manet’s nod to his subject’s identity as an artist.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: Manet kept this portrait of Morisot throughout his life, and it was listed in the inventory of his studio after his death.

title: At the Concert Parisien
artistBio: Georges Seurat entered the École Municipale de Sculpture et de Dessin in Paris at the age of fifteen, where he studied with the sculptor Justin Lequien (1826-1882) and met Aman-Jean. At the École des Beaux-Arts three years later he was taught by Henri Lehmann (1814-1882), a former pupil of Ingres.

artistBioSource.name: Cleveland Museum of Art — artist biography

medium: conté crayon heightened with white chalk on cream handmade modern laid paper

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2607x3400px open-access image (region x=0.2582, y=0.6041, w=0.4212, h=0.2418)

description: Café-concerts were popular places of entertainment for the middle classes in Paris during the late 1800s and usually featured singers or other forms of vaudeville entertainers. Georges Seurat created eight drawings depicting café-concerts, some showing known establishments. This drawing has an innovative viewpoint, in which we peer through the bowler hats of male viewers listening to a female singer on stage.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: Despite Georges Seurat's brief lifespan, he created a large number of drawings, working almost exclusively with the waxy Conté crayon and textured paper used for this sheet.

title: The Red Kerchief
artistBio: Claude Monet spent his youth in Le Havre in Normandy, where his father worked as a wholesale grocer. By the age of sixteen, he had exhibited some of his caricatures in an art supply store, leading to his acquaintance with Boudin.

artistBioSource.name: Cleveland Museum of Art — artist biography

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2732x3400px open-access image (region x=0.3133, y=0.4541, w=0.4198, h=0.2541)

description: This painting depicts Monet's first wife, Camille, outside on a snowy day passing by the French doors of their home at Argenteuil. Her face is rendered in a radically bold Impressionist technique of mere daubs of paint quickly applied, just as the snow and trees are defined by broad, broken strokes of pure white and green.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: Madame Monet’s red cape draws the viewer’s attention beyond the glass of the French doors capturing her glance, a brief moment frozen in time. This painting was very special to Monet and he kept it with him for his entire life.

title: Mademoiselle Louise Riesener in a Hat
artistBio: Born into a prosperous family, Berthe Morisot was encouraged at an early age to become an amateur artist. Along with her sister Edma, she began her studies with Geoffroy-Alphonse Chocarne (act. 1838-1857), a painter trained in the neoclassical tradition.

artistBioSource.name: Cleveland Museum of Art — artist biography

medium: pastel on pale blue laid paper

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 2858x3400px open-access image (region x=0.2705, y=0.3853, w=0.4195, h=0.2647)

description: This portrait depicts Louise Riesener, daughter of artist Léon Riesener and close friend of Morisot. The artist depicted her subject in bust-length profile wearing a black jacket out of which peek the decorative ties of a white blouse. Morisot paid particular attention to the hat; a fashionable Parisian woman of the upper-middle class would have worn such an accessory whenever she went out in public.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: Morisot favored the (formerly) blue paper used here for pastels and used it for numerous works.

title: Hunting near Hartenfels Castle
medium: oil, originally on wood, transferred to masonite

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 3400x2332px open-access image (region x=0.2291, y=0.1278, w=0.3, h=0.3285)

description: The Protestant rulers of Saxony commissioned this animated hunt scene, set near their residence seen in the background, Hartenfels Castle (in eastern Germany). John Frederick the Magnanimous, in the bottom left corner, wears dark green hunting attire; he spans his crossbow and waits for his courtiers and dogs to chase a stag across the river.
license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: Humans, dogs, and deer make up most of the creatures in this busy scene—but not all of them! Look closely at the background to spot a bear and three boars.

title: Study for "Bathers at Asnières"

description: This oil sketch is one of many preparatory studies Seurat made for his monumental painting Bathers at Asnières (1883-84), depicting men leisurely bathing in the Seine near an industrial suburb of Paris. license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
interestingFacts: Seurat’s approach to painting differed greatly from the Impressionist painters who worked outdoors in plein-air. In contrast, he worked in the studio preparing his compositions from drawings and preparatory studies.

title: Christ Crucified Between the Two Thieves: 'The Three Crosses'

title: Saint-Mammès, Loing Canal

title: View of Florence

title: Head of Amenhotep III Wearing the Round Wig

title: Sun Bodhisattva (Nikkō Bosatsu)

title: Rest on the Flight into Egypt

title: Wineglass and a Bowl of Fruit

title: Cupid and Psyche
artistBio: The founder and leading painter of the neoclassical movement in France, Jacques-Louis David was born in Paris to a prosperous family of artists and archi-tects. In 1766 he entered the Académie Royale as the pupil of Joseph-Marie Vien (1716-1809).

artistBioSource.name: Cleveland Museum of Art — artist biography

detail.source: Real crop of the museum's 3400x2574px open-access image (region x=0.4126, y=0.4324, w=0.4209, h=0.4188)

interestingFacts: Jacques-Louis David included two butterflies in this painting: one above the slumbering Psyche and the other on the base of the couple's bed frame.

title: Satyress and Child
